newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany, France at odds on euro conversion methods.
newsitem.headline: Germany, France at odds on euro conversion methods.

text.p: A debate has erupted over how nations participating in economic and monetary union should redenominate outstanding government debt into the euro, the single European currency to be launched on January 1, 1999.
Talks centre on whether government debt converted into euros should be rounded to the nearest euro or to the nearest euro cent, or hundredth of a euro.
German state secretary in the finance ministry Juergen Stark said on Tuesday Finance Minister Theo Waigel had agreed that existing debt should be converted into the euro from its start.

France, which announced long ago it would redenominate its bonds, went a step further, saying it planned to convert outstanding debt by rounding conversions to the nearest euro with cash compensations.

At the European level, no official ruling has been made on redenomination or if the method should be uniform across the euro area, but a recent European Commission report stressed the method should be "easy to implement, fair and cost effective."
The report also said "financial institutions...would prefer the selection of a common approach to redenomination that is transparent and which would cause the fewest secondary effects."
But Germany seems to be leaning toward rounding to the nearest euro cent.

Bankers and analysts in France said the important factor was that a decision had been made on the conversion, clearing the way for Paris to ready itself for 1999. They said France's decision to go with a different conversion system than Germany is expected to choose was less important.
But German economists said the French conversion, the so-called "one euro solution," is less desirable than the "one cent solution" favoured in Germany.

"(The French decision) is very inconvenient," said Ursula Arlt, economist at DG Bank in Frankfurt. "It is typical of the French. They made a premature political announcement that they wanted to redenominate (outstanding debt), but they didn't even address the question of the technical costs."

In Germany, Arlt said detailed disussions on how conversion would work best for the markets led to a commitment to the "one cent solution," before any final decision was made on whether outstanding debt will in fact be converted into euros in 1999.
The two systems appear to have little between them on the surface, but some analysts said small discrepancies could translate into sizeable differences for market particpants.

"There is a potential fortune to be made out of arbitraging these seemingly detailed decisions," said John Butler, WestLB fixed income analyst. "What on the surface is a decision which might change the value of a bond by 0.1 of a pfennig could mean a lot more if you're holding 500 million of them."

Under the "one euro solution," for example, a government bond with a nominal value of 1,000 marks converted into euros at an exchange rate of 0.5238 euros to the mark, would emerge as a bond with a nominal value of 523.8, an awkward number to use as a nominal value in market trading.

"The one euro solution is in the right direction, but does not fully get around the problem of decimal points," said Arlt. "Unmanageable numbers damage the trading situation. Traders cannot deal with them. All these problems can be avoided with the 'one cent solution.'"
But Chris Golden, director and head of fixed income research at Nomura in London, said having round numbers or otherwise was not important for financial markets.

"Since when has any number on the trading floor been manageable?" he said. "Bonds do not trade at 100.00 anyway. So, even if you are trading 100,000 nominal, the actual number underneath is going to be much less pleasant."

Taking the "one cent solution" with the same hypothetical exchange rate, a bond with a nominal value of 1,000 marks would be redenominated as a nominal 52,380 euro cent value and then broken down into individual one-euro cent government bonds.
These tiny one-cent bonds would then be put together in lots of, for example, 100 or 1,000, giving more manageable numbers for trading on exchanges.
Although it would be possible to split nominal values into one euro units, the smaller one-cent unit takes the conversion to a higher number of decimal points and thus, is more precise.
"With (the one-cent solution), the change in economic value with redenomination is kept to an absolute minimum," Golden said.
